title: Five places where enterprise AI stalls on its way to scale
summary: AI pilots and AI transformation are different achievements. A pilot proves the technology works. Scaling it into a shared capability is a separate job, and it's where most initiatives lose steam.
body_markdown:
### You proved AI works. Now it has to work at scale.


Across industries, executives can point to AI initiatives that look, by most measures, successful. Customer service assistants resolve routine inquiries. Generative AI tools summarize documents and draft communications. Predictive models identify risks faster than the processes they replaced.


Even so, the enterprise often hasn't been transformed. AI runs in production across functions and investment keeps rising, yet most organizations report pockets of success rather than enterprise-wide change.


[Gartner](https://www.gartner.com/en/articles/genai-project-failure) puts a number on the drop-off. By the end of 2025, at least half of generative AI projects were abandoned after the proof-of-concept stage. The causes were poor data quality, inadequate risk controls, escalating costs, and unclear business value. Each is a condition of production that a pilot, by design, never has to meet.


*“A proof of concept solves one team’s problem. Transformation has to solve the organization’s.”* — Anthony Martucci, VP, Forward Deployed Engineering, Unisys


A successful pilot answers exactly the question it was built to answer, and that is real progress. It does not tell you whether the result will scale.


### A pilot and a transformation ask different questions


It's tempting to treat a successful pilot as proof that broader transformation is justified, and it's an easy assumption to make. Historically, proving a technology worked was the hardest part of adoption. Once a pilot showed value, wider deployment looked like a matter of time and money.


AI complicates that progression, because a pilot answers a narrow question: Can this technology perform a specific task?


Transformation asks a much broader question: Can this capability be adopted, governed, managed, reused, and scaled across an enterprise?


The distinction sounds subtle, but it decides what happens after the pilot succeeds. The first question is technological, and organizations have become good at answering it. The second is organizational, and organizational problems are the harder kind.


### Call it the AI execution gap


What AI can do and what your organization gets from it is the execution gap, and it’s rarely a technology problem. It opens in five places: context, reuse, visibility, governance, and coordination. All five are organizational, which makes them harder to solve but also puts them within an organization's control.


The AI execution gap opens between AI that works once and AI that works everywhere. It closes when the conditions for scale are handled once and shared, so each use case starts ahead of the last.


1. **Context: AI that understands how the business works**


AI can only work with what it knows. A capable model understands language and patterns. It does not know your organization’s policies, approval thresholds, who is entitled to see what, or the history behind how decisions get made. Some practitioners call this layer an ontology: the structured map of how a business’s concepts, data, and rules relate to one another. The two terms often get used interchangeably right now. Either way, without that map, a model knows only the generic version of your business.


A pilot hides this because it runs inside a narrow slice of the business where somebody has supplied that context by hand. Production gives you no such help. The output then arrives technically sound and operationally wrong, and teams spend their time correcting it.


1. **Reuse: turning one success into many**


One of the most common patterns in enterprise AI is isolated success. A business unit develops a compelling solution, the results are encouraging, and the initiative earns attention across the organization. Then it stalls.


Instead of scaling what worked, other teams start building their own versions. Several groups end up solving similar problems separately, each with their own data, integrations, controls, and operating assumptions.


The organization accumulates AI projects rather than AI capabilities. Value gets created, but it doesn't compound.


1. **Visibility: knowing what AI is doing and what it costs**


Once a capability leaves the pilot and hits daily processes, policies, and complexity, someone has to answer for what it spends, how it performs, how it's secured, and the decisions it shaped.


Most enterprises can answer those questions for one system. Very few can answer them for the portfolio.


1. **Governance: designed in rather than added later**


Innovation tends to move quickly. Governance rarely does. Early experimentation is about speed, and teams are encouraged to test ideas and show value. That's entirely reasonable.


The trouble starts when successful pilots move toward production. Questions that once seemed distant become urgent. Who owns the capability? Who is accountable for its decisions? How should outputs be monitored? What happens when policies change? Which models are approved, and under what circumstances?


Governance is a prerequisite for scale. Building it in at the start costs far less than bolting it onto a capability that's already live.


1. **Coordination: intelligence that works as one system**


Many organizations build AI one use case at a time. A team introduces a knowledge assistant. Another deploys a customer service agent. Somewhere else, a predictive model begins generating insights. Each initiative serves a purpose, and each may perform well on its own.


Zoom out across the enterprise and the picture changes. Customer-facing systems operate separately from internal workflows. Knowledge assistants sit apart from business processes. Data stays fragmented across platforms, departments, and applications.


The result is plenty of intelligence and not enough orchestration. An orchestra made up entirely of talented soloists can still struggle to play a symphony.


### Trust sets the ceiling on what AI delivers


Most AI discussions focus on models, architecture, and automation. The bigger challenge is human. Employees have to know when to trust a system and when to question it. Managers need clarity about who is accountable. Teams need confidence that a new capability supports their work.


A remarkably capable system that no one trusts will struggle to create value. A moderately capable system that's built thoughtfully into existing workflows often will. People decide whether the intelligence a system generates creates value.


### The gap closes at the platform level


It's tempting to solve each of the five gaps locally. Add context to one assistant. Write governance for one model. Build a dashboard for one system. Solved that way, the gap reopens with the next use case, because nothing carries over.


Closing it for good works the other way around. Context, reuse, visibility, governance, and coordination are handled once and shared across every capability, so what an organization learns in one place holds in the next. That's the thinking behind the Unisys Intelligence Accelerator, and it's the difference between running several AI projects and running one system of intelligence.


### Advantage comes from what compounds


Few organizations gain a lasting advantage just because they adopt cloud computing, mobile technology, or data analytics before others. What sets them apart is embedding those capabilities into the way the business operates.


AI is following a similar path. Some organizations will end up with a portfolio of successful projects and isolated wins. Others will build something more repeatable that compounds.


AI pilots continue to show us what's possible. Take your most successful pilot and ask what it would take for a second team to run it next month.


If the answer is rebuilding most of it, that's what the execution gap costs. Closing it starts with knowing which of the five is costing you the most.
